text:
This research looks at how computers can classify sentences, such as analyzing sentiment or sorting questions [P1_p1_c02]. While deep learning has done well in speech recognition and computer vision, natural language processing poses unique challenges [P1_p1_c03]. 

The main idea is using a simple computer vision tool called a convolutional neural network, built on top of pre-trained word vectors [P1_p1_c02][P1_p1_c03]. Word vectors turn words into dense representations that encode semantic features, meaning words with similar meanings stay close together in a vector space [P1_p1_c03]. 

The paper shows that a simple model using static, pre-trained vectors performs remarkably well, competing with more complex deep learning models that require parse trees or complex pooling schemes [P1_p4_c03]. Pre-trained vectors act as good, universal feature extractors across different datasets [P1_p4_c03]. Furthermore, learning task-specific vectors through fine-tuning offers even greater performance gains [P1_p1_c02][P1_p4_c03]. The authors also tested a modified architecture that uses both static and task-specific vectors at the same time [P1_p1_c02][P1_p2_c02]. 

Regarding accuracy, the models improved upon the state of the art on four out of seven tasks tested [P1_p1_c02]. The research shows that unsupervised pre-training of word vectors is an important ingredient for this type of technology [P1_p5_c04]. The sources do not provide data on financial costs or processing speed.
